endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: HDOs should also address how patient opt-out requests are handled.

commentary.bottom_line: No study in the supplied evidence tests whether documenting and flagging patient AI opt-out requests keeps AI from being used against patient wishes, and no study documents how often such requests are lost. The recommendation rests on one governance framework that asks health delivery organizations to address opt-out handling without specifying how.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single endorsement is a framework statement at the should level. It asks organizations to address opt-out handling but does not name documentation or care-team flagging as the method, so the link to this specific practice is indirect.

The supplied support consists of one voluntary governance playbook from CHAI. No statute, federal rule, or agency guidance is included among the sources, so the material provided does not establish a legal requirement to record or flag opt-out requests. Adoption would currently rest on organizational policy.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that measure how often patient AI opt-out requests are recorded, how often a flag reaches the treating team, and how often AI is used after an opt-out despite the flag. Comparisons of recording methods, such as a structured field in the health record versus free-text notes, would show which approach holds up across care transitions and handoffs.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems have no data on whether these patients learn that opt-out is available, can make a request in their language, or have their requests recorded and honored at the same rate as other patients.
